title: Volume of Cylinders, Pyramids, Cones, and Spheres
seo_title: Volume of Cylinders, Cones, Pyramids and Spheres Worksheet (Geometry, G-GMD.A.3) | 100 Questions
standard_text: Use volume formulas for cylinders, pyramids, cones, and spheres to solve problems.
meta_desc: Free Geometry worksheet on volume: cylinders, cones, spheres, hemispheres and pyramids, answers in terms of π, Cavalieri's principle and density. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Cylinder πr²h. Cone ⅓πr²h. Sphere ⁴⁄₃πr³. Pyramid ⅓Bh.
key_sub: Always use the radius. Cones and pyramids are one third of the matching prism or cylinder.
body_html:
How it works

Cylinder: V = πr²h (area of the circle × height). Cone: V = ⅓πr²h, one third of the cylinder with the same base and height. Sphere: V = ⁴⁄₃πr³. A hemisphere is half a sphere: ⅔πr³. Pyramid: V = ⅓Bh, where B is the area of the base.

Cavalieri's principle: two solids with the same height and the same cross-sectional area at every level have the same volume. Density = mass ÷ volume.

Always use the radius. If you are given the diameter, halve it first. An answer “in terms of π” keeps π as a letter, for example 45π cm³.

Example

Cylinder: r = 4 cm, h = 10 cm.

π × 4² × 10 = 160π.

Answer: 502.7 cm³

Example

Cone: r = 3 cm, h = 8 cm.

⅓ × π × 9 × 8 = 24π.

Answer: 75.4 cm³

Example

Sphere: diameter 12 cm.

r = 6 cm.

⁴⁄₃ × π × 216 = 288π.

Answer: 904.8 cm³

Common mistakes

  • Using the diameter instead of the radius.
  • Forgetting the ⅓ in the cone formula.
  • Using 4πr² (surface area) for the volume of a sphere.
  • Mixing units, such as meters and centimeters, in one calculation.

faq.q: What is the formula for the volume of a cone?
faq.a: V = (1/3)πr²h. It is one third of a cylinder with the same base and height.

faq.q: What is the formula for the volume of a sphere?
faq.a: V = (4/3)πr³, where r is the radius.
If two solids have the same height and the same cross-sectional area at every level, they have the same volume.

faq.q: How do you find the volume of a pyramid?
faq.a: Multiply the area of the base by the height and divide by 3: V = (1/3)Bh.

items.q: Two stacks of 13 coins have the same height. One stack is straight and the other leans to one side. Each coin has radius 13 mm and the stacks are 26 mm tall. How do their volumes compare?
c: The straight stack has more volume
The leaning stack has more volume
items.e: Cavalieri's principle: same height and the same cross-section at every level means the same volume. π × 13² × 26 = 4394π. They are equal (4394π mm³ each).
